title: Scale Models and Model Kits
body: A scale model is a physical replica of a real object, built at a fixed ratio such as 1:72 or 1:24. Model kits — plastic snap-together kits, wood ship models, and die-cast collectibles — are the most common form. Scales are written with the model size first: a 1:48 model is one forty-eighth the size of the real thing. Common scales include 1:72 and 1:48 for aircraft, 1:35 for armor, and 1:24 or 1:25 for cars. Building a kit teaches reading plans, gluing, painting, and patience. Start with a simple snap-fit kit before moving to glue-and-paint kits.

title: Architectural Models
body: Architects build physical scale models of buildings to study form, light, and space before construction. Materials include foam board, basswood, museum board, and 3D-printed plastic. Common architectural scales are 1:200 for whole sites, 1:100 for building massing, and 1:50 or 1:20 for detail studies. A good model shows structure, openings, and material changes clearly rather than decorating every surface. White card models are a classic presentation style because they emphasize form over color.

title: Fashion Models — The Profession
body: Fashion models present clothing, accessories, and footwear for designers, photographers, retailers, and advertisers. Categories include runway, editorial, commercial, plus-size, petite, and fit modeling. Models work through agencies that arrange castings and bookings and take a commission. A portfolio of professional photographs is the model's main calling card. The work requires punctuality, physical stamina, and the ability to take direction from photographers and stylists.

title: Role Models
body: A role model is a person whose behavior, achievements, or character others admire and imitate. Role models can be family members, teachers, athletes, scientists, or historical figures. Research in psychology shows that relatable role models — people who overcame obstacles similar to the observer's — are the most motivating. Being a role model carries responsibility: actions speak louder than stated values. Communities often celebrate role models through awards, mentorship programs, and storytelling.

title: Scientific and Computational Models
body: Scientists use models — simplified representations of reality — to explain and predict. A model can be physical (a globe), mathematical (an equation for population growth), or computational (a climate simulation). Good models capture the essential behavior of a system while ignoring irrelevant detail. Models are tested by comparing their predictions against real observations, and refined when they disagree. Famous examples include the Bohr model of the atom, epidemiological SIR models, and general circulation models of climate.

title: Data Models
body: A data model describes how information is organized: the entities, their attributes, and the relationships between them. The relational model organizes data into tables with rows and columns linked by keys. The entity-relationship diagram is the classic design tool for relational databases. Other models include document stores, graph databases, and key-value stores, each suited to different shapes of data. Choosing the right data model is one of the most consequential early decisions in building software.

title: Product Model Naming and Model Numbers
body: Manufacturers identify product lines with model names and numbers: a car has a model year and trim, a phone has a model number like SM-S918. Model numbers often encode generation, region, and configuration. Keeping a clear model-naming scheme helps customers compare products and helps support teams identify exactly which unit a customer owns. Serial numbers are different: they identify one individual unit, while a model number identifies the whole design. Good model naming is short, consistent, and avoids confusing look-alike characters like O and 0.

title: Miniatures, Dioramas, and Wargaming Models
body: Miniature models — from 6mm to 54mm figures — are used in tabletop wargames, dioramas, and dollhouses. Wargaming miniatures are typically cast in plastic, resin, or white metal and painted by hand. A diorama places models in a scenic setting to tell a story, using ground texture, foliage, and backdrops. Common wargaming scales are 28mm and 32mm for skirmish games and 6–15mm for mass battles. Priming, base-coating, washing, and dry-brushing are the core painting techniques.
